modules.title: Past Simple & Continuous
modules.description: Learn to talk about completed actions and ongoing events in the past using the Past Simple and Past Continuous tenses.

lessons.title: Past Simple: Regular Verbs
lessons.description: Form the Past Simple with regular verbs by adding -ed, and learn the three pronunciation rules for the ending.

content.title: How to Form the Past Simple with Regular Verbs

body.html:
To make the Past Simple of a regular verb, add -ed to the base form.

  • work → worked
  • play → played
  • live → lived (the verb already ends in e, so just add -d)
  • stop → stopped (short vowel + single consonant → double the consonant)
  • study → studied (consonant + y → change y to i and add -ed)

Pronunciation of -ed

The -ed ending has three sounds:

  1. /t/ — after voiceless sounds (k, p, f, s, ʃ, tʃ): walked, stopped, laughed
  2. /d/ — after voiced sounds and vowels: played, opened, called
  3. /ɪd/ — after t or d: wanted, needed, started
tips: The -ed spelling rule for 'y' only applies when there is a consonant before 'y'. If there is a vowel before 'y', just add -ed: play → played.
The /ɪd/ pronunciation adds an extra syllable: 'want' is one syllable, but 'wanted' is two.

content.title: Choose the Correct Past Simple Form

body.question: Which is the correct Past Simple form of the verb 'study'?
body.explanation: When a verb ends in consonant + y, change the 'y' to 'i' and add -ed: study → studied.
'Walk' is a regular verb. Add -ed to form the Past Simple: walked.

lessons.title: Past Simple: Irregular Verbs
lessons.description: Learn the most common irregular Past Simple forms — verbs that don't follow the -ed rule.

body.html:
Irregular verbs do not add -ed in the Past Simple. Each verb has its own special past form that you need to memorise.

Common Irregular Verbs

Base FormPast Simple
gowent
seesaw
eatate
havehad
comecame
taketook
makemade
buybought
getgot
givegave

The past form is the same for all subjects: I went, you went, she went, they went.
tips: There is no shortcut — you have to memorise irregular forms. Flashcards and lots of reading help!
Some verbs don't change at all: put → put, cut → cut, read → read (but the pronunciation changes: /riːd/ → /rɛd/).

body.question: What is the Past Simple of 'buy'?
body.explanation: 'Buy' is irregular. Its Past Simple form is 'bought'.

lessons.title: Past Simple: Negatives & Questions
lessons.description: Use 'didn't' to make negatives and 'did' to form questions in the Past Simple.

body.html:
In the Past Simple, we use the auxiliary verb did to make negatives and questions. The main verb goes back to the base form (no -ed, no irregular change).

Negatives

Subject + didn't + base form

  • I didn't go to school. (NOT: I didn't went)
  • She didn't eat breakfast.
  • They didn't play football.

Questions

Did + subject + base form?

  • Did you see the film? (NOT: Did you saw?)
  • Did he come to the party?

Short Answers

  • Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
tips: The most common mistake is using the past form after 'did/didn't'. Always use the BASE form: Did you GO? (not 'Did you went?').
'Was/were' follow their own pattern — they don't use 'did'. We say 'Were you tired?' not 'Did you were tired?'.

body.explanation: To make a Past Simple negative, use 'didn't' + base form: didn't like.

lessons.title: Past Continuous
lessons.description: Describe actions that were in progress at a specific time in the past using was/were + -ing.

content.title: How to Form the Past Continuous

body.html:
The Past Continuous describes an action that was in progress at a particular time in the past.

Form

Subject + was/were + verb-ing

  • I / He / She / It + was + verb-ing
  • You / We / They + were + verb-ing

Examples

  • At 8 p.m., I was watching TV.
  • They were playing football when it started to rain.
  • Was she sleeping when you called?

Past Simple vs Past Continuous

We often use them together: the Past Continuous sets the background scene, and the Past Simple describes the interrupting event.

  • I was walking home when I saw an old friend.
tips: Use 'was' with I/he/she/it and 'were' with you/we/they.
The Past Continuous is NOT used for completed actions. Say 'I watched a film' (finished), not 'I was watching a film' (unless you want to stress that it was in progress).

body.question: Which sentence correctly uses the Past Continuous?
options: They was eating dinner at 7 p.m.
They were eating dinner at 7 p.m.
They were eat dinner at 7 p.m.
body.explanation: 'They' takes 'were' (not 'was'), and the main verb needs the -ing form: were eating.

body.sentence: I ___ (read) a book when the phone rang.
body.explanation: The subject is 'I', so we use 'was' + the -ing form: was reading.

modules.title: Around Town
modules.description: Build practical vocabulary for navigating a town, asking for directions, shopping, and ordering at a restaurant.

lessons.title: Places in Town
lessons.description: Learn the names of common places you can find in a town or city.

body.html:
Here are some important places you will find in most towns:

  • post office — you go here to send letters and parcels
  • bank — you go here to manage your money
  • hospital — you go here when you are very sick or injured
  • pharmacy (also: chemist's in British English) — you buy medicine here
  • supermarket — a large shop where you buy food and household items
  • library — you borrow books here (it's free!)
  • police station — where the police work
  • bus station — where you catch buses to other towns
  • train station (also: railway station) — where you catch trains
  • town hall — the main government building in a town

Useful Patterns

  • Is there a bank near here?
  • Where is the nearest supermarket?
  • I need to go to the post office.
tips: 'Library' means a place to borrow books — it is NOT a bookshop.
In British English, 'chemist's' is more common than 'pharmacy'.

body.question: You need to send a parcel. Where do you go?
body.explanation: You send letters and parcels at the post office.

body.sentence: Excuse me, is there a ___ near here? I need to buy some medicine.
body.explanation: You buy medicine at a pharmacy (or chemist's in British English).

lessons.title: Asking for Directions
lessons.description: Learn how to ask for and give simple directions using key phrases.

body.html:
Asking for Directions

  • Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?
  • Excuse me, where is the nearest bank?
  • Is it far from here?

Giving Directions

  • Go straight (on / ahead).
  • Turn left at the traffic lights.
  • Turn right at the corner.
  • It's on your left / on your right.
  • It's next to the supermarket.
  • It's opposite the bank.
  • It's between the post office and the café.
  • Take the first / second street on the left.

Prepositions of Place

  • next to = beside
  • opposite = on the other side of the street
  • between = in the middle of two things
  • on the corner of = where two streets meet
tips: Always start with 'Excuse me' — it's polite and gets the person's attention.
'Go straight on' (British) and 'Go straight ahead' (American) mean the same thing.

body.translation: Turn left at the traffic lights.

body.question: The bank is ___ the supermarket and the post office.
body.explanation: 'Between' means in the middle of two things. The bank is between the supermarket and the post office.

lessons.title: Shopping
lessons.description: Learn essential vocabulary and phrases for buying things in shops.

body.html:
Key Vocabulary

  • receipt — the piece of paper that shows what you bought and how much you paid
  • change — the money you get back when you pay more than the price
  • cash — coins and banknotes
  • card — a credit or debit card
  • price — how much something costs
  • sale — when things are cheaper than normal
  • size — small (S), medium (M), large (L)
  • fitting room (also: changing room) — where you try on clothes

Useful Phrases

  • How much is this? / How much does this cost?
  • I'd like a large coffee, please.
  • Can I pay by card?
  • Do you have this in a different size?
  • Can I try this on?
  • Can I have a receipt, please?
tips: 'I'd like' is short for 'I would like' — it's more polite than 'I want'.
'How much is this?' (singular) vs 'How much are these?' (plural).

body.sentence: Can I have a ___, please? I need it for returning the item.
body.explanation: A receipt is the paper that proves you bought something. You usually need it to return or exchange items.

body.question: Which is the most polite way to order a coffee?
body.explanation: 'I'd like … please' is the standard polite way to order something.

lessons.title: At the Restaurant
lessons.description: Learn how to order food, understand a menu, and interact with waitstaff.

body.html:
Menu Sections

  • starter (British) / appetiser (American) — a small dish before the main meal
  • main course — the biggest dish
  • dessert — sweet food at the end (cake, ice cream)
  • drinks / beverages

Useful Phrases — Ordering

  • Could I see the menu, please?
  • I'd like the chicken salad, please.
  • For my starter, I'll have the soup.
  • Can I have the bill, please? (British) / Can I have the check, please? (American)

Useful Phrases — Asking Questions

  • What do you recommend?
  • Does this dish contain nuts?
  • Is this vegetarian?
tips: 'Bill' (British English) = 'Check' (American English). Both mean the paper that shows how much you need to pay.
In many English-speaking countries, you usually wait to be seated — don't just sit at any table.

body.translation: I'd like the chicken salad, please.

body.sentence: Could I have the ___, please? We're ready to pay.
body.explanation: In British English we say 'bill'; in American English we say 'check'.

modules.title: Daily Life Phrasal Verbs
modules.description: Learn essential phrasal verbs used in everyday situations — searching, transport, errands, and movement.

lessons.title: Look For & Find Out
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs related to searching for things and discovering information.

body.html:
look for

Meaning: to try to find something or someone.

  • I'm looking for my keys. Have you seen them?
  • She's looking for a new job.

'Look for' is not the same as 'look at' (= direct your eyes at something).

find out

Meaning: to discover or learn new information.

  • I need to find out what time the train leaves.
  • She found out that the shop was closed on Sundays.

'Find out' is about information. 'Find' alone is about objects: I found my keys (= I have them now).

look up

Meaning: to search for information in a book, dictionary, or online.

  • I looked up the word in a dictionary.
  • Can you look up the opening hours on their website?
tips: 'Look for' = search. 'Look at' = see/watch. 'Look after' = take care of. Don't mix them up!
With 'find out' and 'look up', a pronoun goes in the middle: 'look it up', 'find it out'.

body.sentence: I don't know the answer. Let me ___ it ___ online.
body.explanation: 'Look up' means to search for information in a reference source. When using a pronoun, it goes in the middle: look it up.

body.question: She found out that her flight was cancelled. What does 'found out' mean?
body.explanation: 'Find out' means to discover or learn new information. She discovered that her flight was cancelled.

lessons.title: Pick Up & Drop Off
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs related to transport, collecting things, and running errands.

body.html:
pick up

Meaning 1: to lift something from a surface.

  • He picked up the book from the floor.

Meaning 2: to collect someone (usually in a car).

  • I'll pick you up at the station at 6 p.m.

drop off

Meaning: to take someone or something to a place and leave them there.

  • Can you drop me off at the supermarket?
  • I need to drop off this parcel at the post office.

get on / get off

get on — to board (a bus, train, plane).

  • We got on the bus at Park Street.

get off — to leave (a bus, train, plane).

  • Get off at the next stop.

Note: For cars and taxis, we use get in and get out (of).
tips: Use 'get on/off' for large vehicles (bus, train, plane) and 'get in/out of' for small vehicles (car, taxi).
With pronouns, the object goes in the middle: 'pick her up', 'drop him off'.

body.question: I need to ___ my sister ___ at the airport. Her flight arrives at 3 p.m.
body.explanation: 'Pick up' means to collect someone, usually in a car. You pick someone up when they arrive.

body.translation: Get off at the next stop.

lessons.title: Come Back & Go Out
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs about movement — leaving, returning, and going places.

body.html:
come back

Meaning: to return to a place.

  • What time will you come back?
  • She came back from holiday last week.

go out

Meaning: to leave your home for entertainment or social activities.

  • Do you want to go out for dinner tonight?
  • They go out every Saturday night.

get back

Meaning: to return (similar to 'come back' but more informal).

  • I got back home at midnight.
  • When did you get back from your trip?

set off

Meaning: to start a journey.

  • We need to set off early to avoid traffic.
  • They set off at 6 a.m.
tips: 'Come back' and 'get back' are very similar. 'Come back' is slightly more formal.
'Go out' can also mean to have a romantic relationship: 'Are they going out?' = 'Are they dating?'

body.sentence: A: What time did you ___ ___ from work? B: About 7 p.m.
body.explanation: 'Get back' or 'come back' both mean to return. 'Get back' is slightly more informal and natural here.

body.question: We need to set off early tomorrow. What does 'set off' mean?
body.explanation: 'Set off' means to start a journey or leave for a destination.
